title: Social media
hookLine: post as if Christ were reading
tomorrow: Abuela prays all through the evening news. does it help anyone?

cards: A clip from the game: the other team's keeper slips, the ball rolls in, and somebody in the stands caught every second of it. It's funny, honestly. Everyone in the stands saw it anyway.
A caption writes itself, and a clip like that could travel far by morning. The thumb is already on share. Post it or not?
This is a choice from an ordinary week, and the tradition has a test for it that fits in a caption box.

teach.b: Paul wrote it long before anyone posted anything, in his letter to the Ephesians.

In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth; but that which is good, to the edification of faith, that it may administer grace to the hearers." Three tests in one verse. Is it good?
Does it build up? Does it give something to the people who hear it? A post has more hearers than a mouth ever did.

Jesus turns the same thing into a mirror: "All things therefore whatsoever you would that men should do to you, do you also to them." The keeper in the clip will see it too, or her little brother will.

Pope Francis wrote that the digital world can be rich in humanity, a network not of wires but of people. That's the shift. The question stops being will it get views, and becomes who's on the other end.
In Matthew, Jesus says that what's done to the least of his brethren is done to him.
So the test in the outline, post as if Christ were reading, has a second edge: he's also the one in the clip.

teach.h: HE'S ALSO THE ONE IN THE CLIP.
teach.b: Would he post it isn't a ban on jokes.
Plenty of funny things build people up. It's a pause long enough to see the person.

how: The Church marks a World Day of Social Communications each year, with a papal message on media; Catholics apply the eighth commandment and the golden rule to what they post.

o: a private diary kept locked away
a parish newsletter printed on paper
a crowd you can speak to in seconds

games.q: the caption-box test — tap the pairs.
p: only what builds up the hearers
do as you'd have done to you
a network not of wires but of people
done to the least, done to him

s: Paul says speech should build up and give grace to the hearers
Ephesians 4:29: that it may administer grace to the hearers.
the golden rule covers what you do, not what you post
all things whatsoever: a post is something done to someone.
Pope Francis called the digital world a place with no real humanity
he wrote that it can be rich in humanity: a network not of wires but of people.

games.q: your cousin's wedding toast went badly, and your aunt wants to post the video 'because it's hilarious.' what does today's test say?
o: ask your cousin first, and leave it unposted if it'd shame him.
post it; it's family, so teasing is part of the deal.
post it with a sweet caption so it comes off kind.
games.why: Paul's test is what builds up the hearers, and your cousin is one of them. a kind caption doesn't change what the clip does to him.

practice: Hold your phone in an open hand, screen dark, thumb resting off it. Bring to mind the last thing you posted or shared, and the faces of the people who saw it, one or two at a time. Ask of each one quietly: did it build them up?
Then set the phone down, screen side down, and let your hands rest empty.

wordCard.voice: Social media. A crowd you can speak to in seconds, every word landing on a real person somewhere, including the one in the clip.

orig.note: Greek: building up. Paul's word in Ephesians 4:29, rendered edification in the Douay-Rheims.

carryVoice: Your line: would he post it. A pause long enough to see the person on the other end. Till tomorrow.

sources.q: Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth; but that which is good, to the edification of faith, that it may administer grace to the hearers.
All things therefore whatsoever you would that men should do to you, do you also to them.

sources.ref: Francis, Message for the 48th World Communications Day (2014)
